## Introduction

An ordination places samples on a few axes so that similar samples land near
each other, ready to plot. ecodive has ten ordination methods, and two
functions that show which features or variables drive the axes. All of them
are written in parallel C and give the same results as the R and Python
packages they replace, for any number of threads.

Most methods ordinate a distance matrix, which you compute first with any
beta diversity metric. Two methods, PCA and robust Aitchison PCA, start from
the count table itself.

```
                 bray(), beta_div(), ...
  count table  ────────────────────────►  dm  ──►  dist_ord(dm, 'pcoa')
       │                                           pcoa(dm), nmds(dm), umap(dm), ...
       │                                           dist_test(dm, 'permanova', ...)
       │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────►  count_ord(counts, 'pca')
                                                   pca(counts), rpca(counts)
```

The examples here use R's built-in `iris` data: 150 flowers (the samples),
four measurements of each (the features), and three species. Your own data
can be any count table that ecodive takes, such as a matrix, a sparse
matrix, or a `phyloseq` or `rbiom` object.

```{r}
library(ecodive)

head(iris)

dm <- bray(iris[, 1:4])
```


## Choosing a method

| Function     | Method                                         | Input  | Best for                                                                 |
| :----------- | :--------------------------------------------- | :----- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pcoa()`     | Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA)          | `dm`   | The default: exact, fast, and reports the variance on each axis.        |
| `mds()`      | Metric Multidimensional Scaling                | `dm`   | Fitting the distances themselves in exactly `n_axes` dimensions.        |
| `nmds()`     | Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS)     | `dm`   | Keeping the rank order of distances; popular with Bray-Curtis.          |
| `isomap()`   | Isometric Feature Mapping (Isomap)             | `dm`   | Long gradients that PCoA bends into an arch.                            |
| `tsne()`     | t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding    | `dm`   | Separating clusters; distances between clusters mean little.            |
| `umap()`     | Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection  | `dm`   | Clusters, with more of the global layout kept than t-SNE.               |
| `dbrda()`    | Distance-based Redundancy Analysis (db-RDA)    | `dm`   | Axes that sample metadata explain (a constrained ordination).           |
| `capscale()` | Constrained Analysis of Principal Coordinates  | `dm`   | The same, as `vegan::capscale()` computes it.                           |
| `pca()`      | Principal Component Analysis (PCA)             | counts | Euclidean geometry of (transformed) counts, with feature loadings.      |
| `rpca()`     | Robust Aitchison PCA                           | counts | Sparse compositional data, such as microbiome counts.                   |

`list_dist_ords()` lists the methods that take distances, with the other
names each one answers to.


## The result

Every method returns the same kind of object: a matrix with one row per
sample and one column per axis, so it goes straight into `plot()` or a data
frame.

```{r}
ord <- pcoa(dm)
head(ord)
```

Its attributes say how the ordination was made and how good it is. They
always begin with `method`, `eig` (the eigenvalues), and `prop` (the
proportion of variance on each axis), followed by the method's own.

```{r}
str(ord)
```

`prop` makes informative axis labels. PCoA axes share one scale, so plot
them with `asp = 1` to keep distances true.

```{r}
pct <- round(100 * attr(ord, 'prop'), 1)

plot(
  ord, col = iris$Species, asp = 1,
  xlab = paste0('PCoA1 (', pct[1], '%)'),
  ylab = paste0('PCoA2 (', pct[2], '%)') )
legend('topleft', levels(iris$Species), col = 1:3, pch = 1)
```


## Running methods by name

`dist_ord()` runs any distance-based method by name, as `beta_div()` does
for beta diversity metrics. Each method keeps its own arguments and
defaults, and `seed` is accepted (and ignored) by the methods that have no
random parts, so one call can run them all.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
ords <- list(
  'PCoA'   = dist_ord(dm, 'pcoa'),
  'MDS'    = dist_ord(dm, 'mds',    seed = 1),
  'NMDS'   = dist_ord(dm, 'nmds',   seed = 1),
  'Isomap' = dist_ord(dm, 'isomap', n_neighbors = 50),
  't-SNE'  = dist_ord(dm, 'tsne',   seed = 1),
  'UMAP'   = dist_ord(dm, 'umap',   seed = 1) )

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
for (nm in names(ords))
  plot(ords[[nm]], col = iris$Species, main = nm, xlab = '', ylab = '')
```

Names are matched forgivingly, so `'PCoA'`, `'cmdscale'`, `'metaMDS'`, and
`'t-SNE'` all work. Finished code should use the primary names shown by
`list_dist_ords('id')`.

```{r}
list_dist_ords()
```


## Non-Euclidean distances

Many ecological distances, such as Bray-Curtis and unweighted UniFrac, are
not Euclidean: PCoA then finds negative eigenvalues, which cannot be drawn.
`correction = 'lingoes'` or `'cailliez'` adds the smallest constant that
removes them, as `ape::pcoa()` does.

```{r}
ord <- pcoa(dm, correction = 'cailliez')
attr(ord, 'constant')
```

NMDS sidesteps the question by fitting only the rank order of the
distances. Its `stress` attribute measures how well it did: below 0.1 is
good, and below 0.05 is excellent.

```{r}
attr(nmds(dm), 'stress')
```


## Constrained ordination

`dbrda()` and `capscale()` find the axes of `dm` that sample metadata
explain. Give one variable as `groups`, or several in a `formula`.

```{r}
ord <- dbrda(dm, 'Species', iris)

attr(ord, 'r_squared')

attr(ord, 'centroids')
```

The first two axes (`dbRDA1`, `dbRDA2`) are constrained by species, and the
third (`MDS1`) is the largest remaining variation. A formula can hold
several variables, and `Condition()` removes the effect of one before the
others are fitted, as in `vegan`.

```{r}
ord <- dbrda(dm, data = iris, formula = ~ Species + Condition(Sepal.Width))
attr(ord, 'inertia')
```


## Ordinating counts directly

`pca()` and `rpca()` take the count table rather than distances.
`count_ord()` runs them by name, as `dist_ord()` does for the methods that
take distances: `count_ord(counts, 'pca')` is `pca(counts)`. PCA
works on any of ecodive's transformations, such as `norm = 'clr'` (centered
log-ratios, with a `pseudocount` for zeros) or `norm = 'hellinger'`
(square-root proportions, a common choice for community data);
`scale = TRUE` gives every
feature equal weight. The `loadings` attribute holds each feature's
direction, for a biplot.

```{r}
ord <- pca(iris[, 1:4], scale = TRUE)

attr(ord, 'loadings')

load <- attr(ord, 'loadings') * 3
plot(ord, col = iris$Species, asp = 1)
arrows(0, 0, load[, 1], load[, 2], length = 0.1)
text(load[, 1:2], labels = rownames(load), pos = 4)
```

PCA is PCoA of Euclidean distances: both give the same scores, up to each
axis's sign. `pca()` also returns the loadings, and never forms the
150-by-150 distance matrix.

```{r}
all.equal(abs(pca(iris[, 1:4])[, 1]), abs(pcoa(euclidean(iris[, 1:4]))[, 1]))
```

`rpca()` is robust Aitchison PCA (as in the `gemelli` Python package and
QIIME 2's DEICODE). It treats zeros as missing rather than adding a
pseudocount, which suits sparse microbiome counts.

```{r}
ord <- rpca(iris[, 1:4])
round(100 * attr(ord, 'prop'), 1)
```


## What drives the axes?

`pcoa_biplot()` projects each feature of a table onto a PCoA, giving an
arrow for each one, as scikit-bio does.

```{r}
ord    <- pcoa(dm)
scores <- pcoa_biplot(ord, iris[, 1:4])
scores
```

`envfit()` fits sample metadata, or a feature table, onto any ordination.
Numeric variables get an arrow and r-squared, factors a centroid per level,
and each one a permutation p-value, as `vegan::envfit()` gives.

```{r}
fit <- envfit(ord, iris)
fit

# An arrow for each measurement, longer for a better fit.
vec <- fit[is.na(fit$level), ]
xy  <- vec[, c('PCoA1', 'PCoA2')] * sqrt(vec$r2) * 0.1
plot(ord, col = iris$Species, asp = 1)
arrows(0, 0, xy$PCoA1, xy$PCoA2, length = 0.1)
text(xy, labels = vec$variable, pos = 1, cex = 0.8)
```


## Speed and reproducibility

Every method runs on all available cores by default; set `cpus` to use
fewer. Results are identical for any number of threads. Methods with random
starts (`mds()`, `nmds()`, `tsne()`, and `umap()`) take a `seed`, so a seed
always gives the same result.

```{r}
identical(nmds(dm, seed = 1, cpus = 1), nmds(dm, seed = 1, cpus = 2))
```


## Next steps

An ordination shows whether groups of samples look different. To test it,
see `vignette('stat_tests')`.
